cards.context: Mandel此前凭借《Station Eleven》获得巨大声誉，该书描写全球流感疫情后的文明重建，在2020年新冠疫情期间被广泛重新阅读。她的新作延续了对社会崩溃与重建的思考，但将焦点从瘟疫转向美国政治分裂。

cards.source_text: When Emily St John Mandel was a child she had a dream that would stay with her for decades. It was a nightmare in which “I was trying to find my dad in a crowd, and there were other people who looked like him but weren’t him”, she says. “It just kind of struck my imagination.” Forty-ish years later, Mandel’s seventh novel, Exit Party, opens with a gathering in Los Angeles, 2031, where bizarre things happen. Doubles of some guests appear. Someone else disappears altogether. The novel then alternates between two potential future Americas, one riven by the chaos of civil war, the other a surveillance state. Doppelgangers and alternative realities are having a cultural moment in our uncanny, deepfake times. Mandel says the biggest challenge western democracy faces is “the collapse of consensual reality. When you get to a situation where half the electorate disagrees on basic reality – for example, who won an election, or is Covid real? I don’t know how you come back from that.” On a more personal level, she has always been fascinated by what she calls “the counter-life – the one where you took a different job or married a different person. The way that, if we made a different decision, we would have become a somewhat different person.” This interest comes, she thinks, from a feeling that “my life as a writer in New York City is a bit improbable”. Mandel was home-schooled on a tiny island in British Columbia, Canada, before training as a dancer. As she puts it, she was “essentially not educated until I was about 15 … I haven’t got a high school diploma.” She wrote while working office jobs until her third novel, Station Eleven, became a smash hit. The 2014 story of life after a global pandemic felt so prescient when readers rediscovered it during Covid that she developed a reputation for clairvoyance. It has sold 1.5m copies and been translated into 37 languages. Her novels since – The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility – were global bestsellers too. It’s a staggering career, and, as she sees it: “There are a million ways this might not have happened.” We meet on a sunny New York City day, in the lobby of a sleek Williamsburg hotel. Mandel, who lives in nearby Queens, wears a rose-printed shirt and comes across as warm yet precise. She’s off to have a haircut after we meet, even though her neat pixie cut scarcely looks trimmable. cards.source_text: The more power the radical rightwing nationalists of our age accrue, the greater the risk that their destructive brand of politics becomes normalised. We should not, for instance, regard it as normal that the man in charge of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals casually promises “a whole civilisation will die tonight”. We should not accept that history’s first trillionaire is allowed to spread racist conspiracy theories to a hitherto unimaginable extent. We should be alarmed that, here in the UK, a party tipped to lead a potential future government is trying to cruise to power in the slipstream of this international movement. In fact, we shouldn’t just be alarmed by such developments: we should stop them and urgently repair the damage already done. But how? And what is the nature of that damage? This bold, clarifying intervention from Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor provides some of the answers. “End times fascism” is their term for a convergence of interests that can broadly be understood as a response to the climate crisis. Faced with a world coming under unprecedented strain from environmental shocks and an unequal, resource-hungry economic system, today’s reactionaries are effectively saying: bring it on. “The most powerful people in the world are preparing for the end of the world, an end they themselves are frenetically accelerating,” Klein and Taylor write, describing a loose alliance of three principal factions rooted in US political and business elites. First are the religious fanatics who see each new disaster as a welcome sign we are entering the end of days, but find common ground with secular demagogues who promise a glorious, prosperous future on the ruins of our present. Think, for instance, of the mirage of a “New Gaza”, a property developers’ fever dream that the Trump administration – heavily influenced by Christian Zionists – claims will arise from the wreckage of Israel’s US-backed genocide. Next are the new tech barons, who preach that only the AI “arms race”, as Klein and Taylor put it, can save humanity – even as its demand for water and electricity scorches the planet – while they themselves dream of sitting out societal breakdown in remote, fortified enclaves. Last come the political entrepreneurs who transform visions of disaster into votes by promising to turn their nations into bunkered garrison states. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 19 minute listen I am at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing from enormous eyes like sprinkles. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces the tears before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue. This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media. Children’s media are usually judged by their content and quantity: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial or safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations, or toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots (2016-20), the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work, or where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information. Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 23 minute listen This semester, my students are learning about four polymaths who shaped Islamic science: al-Biruni, Alhazen, Avicenna and al-Khwarizmi. Their circumstances could hardly have been more different: one wrote his way out of scarcity; one was held under house arrest for a decade; one distilled an era’s medical knowledge into a text that ruled European universities for 500 years; and the last worked at the largest research institution of his age. But each shared the same underlying instinct: to move freely between mathematics, medicine, astronomy, philosophy and poetry, testing one discipline’s assumptions against another’s. My classroom is in Pakistan, where students arrive eager to talk about disruption and employability, but rarely about breadth. I want them to see, through these four lives, that this kind of expansiveness isn’t a luxury for stable times; it has produced some of the most enduring breakthroughs in the history of science. After 15 years working in liberal arts education, I believe a reintegration of disciplines in a Hellenistic style can lead the way. I’m not making a superficial case for ‘interdisciplinarity’. Instead, I’m arguing for something more specific: the recovery of the penchants of polymathy that once thrived in the Muslim world. Rather than fetishising disruptive innovation through compulsory courses on entrepreneurship and applied methods, we should offer an entirely different model of how to learn and what learning is for – especially since my students already enter university with a narrowly vocational mindset. The word polymathy itself captures the bricolage of many (poly) worlds of knowledge (mathy). Polymathy offers respite and reflection in a world fractured by war, climate catastrophe and injustice. It is sourced from indigenous idioms of the Muslim world rather than an imposition by the Global North. Today, polymathy brings different kinds of thinking to bear on political, economic and environmental problems. At a time when students are reading less of the classic canon and worrying more about employment opportunities, the expansiveness of polymathy can offer a meaningful path forward. These are the lessons of the great Islamic polymaths. The life of our opening actor al-Biruni has much to teach students about the human dimensions of science. cards.source_text: ‘What do you think this movie is about?’ In this video essay, the US filmmaker Kevin B Lee recalls the shock of seeing, as a young film buff, the raw, violent and widely acclaimed Vietnam War film Platoon (1986) with his family in a San Francisco cinema. Recording outside the building that once housed that cinema, he details his harrowing time in the theatre and the film’s reverberations in his life beyond the theatre’s walls, including how it stirred generational trauma in his family and racism at school. With his deceptively simple approach, Lee inverts and subverts Oliver Stone’s epic, crafting, on a shoestring budget, a profound and intensely personal meditation on memory. Lee’s video essay was published as part of ‘Once Upon a Screen’, a series of video essays about film viewing and childhood trauma, commissioned and curated by Ariel Avissar and Evelyn Kreutzer, for The Cine-Files journal of cinema studies, Issue 15.

cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. Later, while working on the Imperial Hotel between 1917 and 1922, he spent a total of more than three years there, later writing that “the pursuit of the Japanese print became my constant recreation while in Tokio,” a quest whose “adventures and excursions would take place at night or sometimes call for a journey by day to distant places.” This positioned him well to take on a sideline as a dealer (or as he liked to call himself, a merchant) of Japan

cards.source_text: In some rare cases, adaptations and interpretations of a literary work can surpass the source. Despite hundreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, filmmakers, game/toy designers, and radio producers, this has never been true of the fully-realized fantasy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings trilogy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we noted in a previous post, Tolkien’s fictional world is so intricate, its sources so vast and varied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Professor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to students and curious readers, such as with his eight-part lecture series on The Hobbit. One might also add illustrators to the list of Tolkien interpreters above who have—in the almost ninety years since The Hobbit’s publication and more than seventy years since the first appearance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visualize Tolkien’s world. But perhaps no one did so better than the master himself. Long known as a visual artist as well as a literary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illustrations for The Hobbit, one of which adorns 2011’s HarperCollins 75th anniversary edition of the book. He also created these original cover designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. In the long and complex publication history of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books published during his lifetime, but the sigil in the center of The Fellowship of the Ring design (above), with its ominous eye of Sauron surrounded by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the elegant, minimalist covers of the first edition of the trilogy. Tolkien’s artwork received a thorough treatment in a 1995 monograph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illustrator, which covers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the magic of flickr brings us this compendium of Tolkien illustrations. Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2013. The annual meeting of the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC) concluded on Sept. 4 with an agreement to adopt a long-term harvest strategy for Pacific bluefin tuna. The agreement aims to ensure sustainable management of this species, which has only recently recovered after decades of overfishing. But the commission fell short of establishing a harvest strategy for other tuna species — bigeye, skipjack and yellowfin — managed under the convention. “A proposal was adopted … and that’s really great progress,” Dave Gershman, a senior officer for international fisheries at the U.S.-based think tank The Pew Charitable Trusts, who took part in the meeting as an observer, told Mongabay. The commission approved the plan for Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis) after 10 years of research and mediation. The plan establishes science-based rules to support the stock’s complete recovery and long-term protection while taking into account impacts on the broader ecosystem. “You want to have these things in place when times are good so it’s there when you need it,” Gershman said. The 104th meeting of the IATTC took place in Lisbon from Aug. 31 to Sept. 4. cards.source_text: Scientists have discovered nine new deep-sea sponge species off Alaska, offering new insights into the region’s largely unexplored marine biodiversity. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) announced the discovery on Thursday, saying the species were found in the Gulf of Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. The findings bring the total number of known sponge species in Alaska to 232. The specimens were collected during Noaa Fisheries’ annual bottom-trawl surveys, which monitor groundfish and shellfish stocks. Researchers analyzed samples collected as far back as 2012, describing the new species in two recent scientific papers. Often described as living water pumps, sponges are among Earth’s earliest multicellular animals, dating back more than 600m years. They filter seawater and help create habitats on the seafloor, despite having no brain or complex organs. “Sponges are ecologically important,” said Sean Rooney, a Noaa fisheries biologist and co-author of the studies at the agency’s Alaska Fisheries Science Center. “They aren’t plants, but like trees in a forest, they provide complex structure along the seafloor that creates habitat and refuge for commercially important fish and crabs,” he added. “Each time we find a new species, it opens up new doors … Deep water is hard to access, especially rocky places we can’t reach with bottom-trawl surveys. There are now more than 232 identified species of sponges in Alaska, and probably hundreds more that we don’t know about yet. The future in this field is exciting,” he continued. Unlike most marine animals, which can be identified by visible traits such as fins and body shapes, sponges can be much harder to distinguish. Because they lack complex organs and other distinctive external features, scientists often rely on their microscopic skeletons and genetic material to identify them. “DNA barcodes provide a quick genetic reference,” said Meredith Everett, a biologist at Noaa’s Northwest Fisheries Science Center. “Sponge DNA can be tricky because they filter-feed, and within their tissues we may find foreign DNA and biochemicals that inhibit testing. But despite the challenges, we successfully developed several new barcodes for Alaskan species,” she added. Her job is to scare them back into the burrows.” Jojo – a five-year-old kelpie/jack russell/whippet cross – has been helping staff locate and map warrens so they can be fumigated or ripped up. There is an ongoing battle at Bon Bon to keep rabbit numbers in check, especially after rain. Fresh shoots of native plants including acacia and mulga should be providing habitat for native species but are instead becoming food and breeding fuel for rabbits. The population growth at Bon Bon and Boolcoomatta reserve to the east, is being repeated around Australia. The European rabbit, Oryctolagus cuniculus, is one of Australia’s worst feral pests. After a wet winter in central and southern parts of the country, their numbers are booming. “We’ve noticed increases all around the country,” says the director of research, development and engagement at the Centre for Invasive Species Solutions, Dr John Virtue. In particular, Virtue points to rabbit hotspots in southern parts of Western Australia, suburban Canberra; peri-urban areas around Adelaide; the New South Wales Riverina; and southern Queensland. In Albany in southern WA, rabbits at “plague-levels” have invaded farms and one of the country’s top golf courses. Greens on the golf course had as many as 30 rabbits “having a party” each evening and grounds staff have been battling to fill holes dug by the rabbits. “They can get to incredible numbers and you see the whole landscape gets denuded,” Virtue says. From 24 to 200 million Though they were introduced on the first fleet during the British invasion in 1788, research has traced the species’ continent-wide spread to one consignment of 24 rabbits brought in to the country by a settler, Thomas Austin, in 1859. By the 1920s, rabbits had reached plague proportions, with estimates numbering them in their billions. More recent counts put the current population at closer to 200 million but the true number is unknown as there is no formal monitoring. Their impact on the landscape has been measured. The Buriganga River, which flows by Dhaka city, is one of Bangladesh’s most polluted waterways and ranks among the most contaminated urban rivers in the world. Every day, the 29-kilometre- (18-mile-) long Buriganga River absorbs toxic industrial effluent from hundreds of factories, continuous tannery discharges, untreated sewage and solid waste, leaving much of the river virtually lifeless for fish. However, in the Buriganga, where native fish species have essentially vanished, endangered Ganges river dolphins (Platanista gangetica) continue to persist. A recent study published in the Journal of Asia-Pacific Biodiversity found that around 20 dolphins live in the river. Researchers conducted the study for 12 months, from September 2023 to August 2024, and systematically surveyed a 27-km (16.7-mi) stretch of this heavily polluted river that skirts the southern edge of Dhaka. “The Buriganga is not a usual place for dolphins, where native fishes have largely vanished. Leaving the river full of invasive suckermouth catfish [Hypostomus Plecostomus, locally called sakar fish],” one of the researchers, Md. Aminur Rahman, told Mongabay. “When we found [the dolphins], we were amazed at how it was possible. Because the river is not livable for fish. Around the year, we didn’t track any dolphins only during two of the months, but all the other 10 months we tracked them.” The highest number of dolphins were seen in December, and throughout the winter season, and none were seen in October 2023 or between July and August of 2024. The dolphin groups averaged 4.18 individuals, higher than in earlier reports, and calves accounted for nearly 16% of the sightings, indicating that reproduction continues despite the extreme pollution conditions. cards.source_text: - In Panama, various initiatives are underway to reduce bycatch of sharks and rays, led by biologists, NGOs, politicians, and local restaurants. - Many industrial fishing boats carry biologists with them to help train the crew on how to free marine animals accidentally caught in their nets. - A bill is also currently in discussion in the legislature that proposes measures to restore and conserve shark and ray populations. - According to local experts, the bill would mark a major step forward for shark conservation, but still has significant weaknesses because the country lacks data on shark and ray populations, especially on breeding sites. PUERTO CAIMITO, Panama — It’s a late April morning and the Tabor, an industrial fishing boat, is sailing around Chepillo Island in Panama Bay. Under the eyes of the crew, Yehudi Rodríguez, a marine biologist specializing in sharks, and sailor Joel Cordoba free a large black devil ray from a purse seine net and launch it back into the water. As they work with the biologist, the sailors, around a dozen of them, joke among themselves. Tabor is part of the Promarina S.A. fleet, a Panamanian company that produces fish oil and fish meal, authorized to catch only small open-ocean fish, or pelagics, such as sardines and herrings. Every two weeks, Rodríguez, a professor of biology at the University of Panama and director of the Shark Defenders NGO, analyzes bycatch — marine species not targeted but accidentally caught by fishers — freeing sharks, rays, and other animals entangled in the purse seine nets of Promarina vessels. “It’s an emotion to see a huge Mobula for the first time and liberate it in the ocean,” Rodríguez, 49, tells Mongabay after freeing the devil ray, which weighed an estimated 100 kilograms (220 pounds). Just a few hours later, Hermes, 18, the youngest sailor on the crew and nicknamed Mbappé after the French football star, helps Rodríguez liberate another ray, both taking care to avoid being hit by the animal’s venomous barb. Before returning an animal into the water, Rodríguez follows a short protocol: she records the coordinates of the bycatch location, identifies the species, takes its measurements and a tissue sample, then tags it. But if the rescued animal is in extreme danger, the release is immediate. Rodríguez has been working on this project for five years, during which nearly 407 individual animals, including sharks and rays, have been tagged. cards.source_text: This summer has been challenging for the fruit trees in my garden, with intense heat and a lack of rain causing poor cropping, premature ripening and pre-harvest drop. While my dessert and cooking apples have produced just a handful of stunted, crab-apple-sized fruit, and my quince is bare, the Victoria plum growing next to the greenhouse is the exception. Its branches are so heavily laden that several have snapped under the weight. For the past week, I’ve been plucking and eating the plums straight from the tree. Occasionally, as I’ve bitten into them, the soft, honeyed flesh has given way to the bitter taste and gritty texture of coffee grounds. I assumed the woody endocarp that protects the seed had started to break down, perhaps due to environmental stress. It wasn’t until I cut one open and pulled out the pit, revealing a small, vivid pink caterpillar surrounded by crumbly brown pellets, that I realised I had been ingesting frass – insect excrement. The culprits were the larvae of the plum fruit moth (Grapholita funebrana), a drab, greyish-brown species that is locally common in southern England. In mid-summer, females lay individual eggs on developing fruit, and when the creamy-white, brown-headed caterpillars hatch, they burrow in, feasting on the flesh around the stone. As they grow and mature, their bodies flush pink. From a distance, the dusky purple plums looked flawless. Upon closer inspection, I discovered that affected fruit were slightly misshapen, and there was often a globule of clear, sticky sap oozing from the barely visible entry hole – a defence mechanism known as gummosis, triggered when the caterpillar bores into the skin. I usually leave fallen fruit for the blackbirds, peacock butterflies and wasps. But to prevent the caterpillars from emerging, pupating and perpetuating the cycle, the advice is to remove all dropped and damaged plums, disposing of them well away from the tree. I salvaged what I could to make jam, consigning the infested scraps to the compost bin. The following morning, I came into the kitchen to find a squirming mass of caterpillars had migrated out of the fruit and on to the bin lid.
cards.source_title: Country diary: Notice anything wrong with this ripe, succulent plum? | Claire Stares

cards.source_text: When Sylvan Esso’s self-titled debut dropped in 2014, their electronic songcraft felt novel. It played like a triangulation of Tune-Yards’ digital playground-chants, Everything But the Girl’s soul-folk remixes, and the sing-song indie-pop of Feist, with whom vocalist Amelia Meath toured as backup singer and opener with her woodsy harmony trio Mountain Man. If Sylvan Esso once scanned as a fusion experiment, it now reflects the science of pop, indie or otherwise: idiosyncratic, beat-built, and prone to occasional mea-culpa cultural critiques (an electronic pop tradition from the get-go). What’s always made the group special is Meath’s voice—a bit scuffed, faintly parched but lithe, playful and harmonically on-point, warmly human even when sonically distressed, which it often is. It’s a nice voice to be around, as a listener and, evidently, as an in-demand collaborator: Recently, she’s covered Mazzy Star with Gregory Alan Isakov and Broken Social Scene with Maggie Rogers; she also sung backup on Tyler Childers’ Snipe Hunter and Kevin Morby’s Little Wide Open. No score yet, be the first to add. Ow ∞ is an especially coherent Sylvan Esso album. Unsettled though it is, it boasts a clearer emotional arc than past sets and production that feels particularly fine-tuned, maybe the result of the four-year gap since No Rules Sandy. Per usual, those productions, built with co-pilot Nick Sanborn, give Meath’s voice space to shapeshift and work out its shit, which here seems to involve of-the-moment quandaries: How do you function in a hydrant-flow of current-event horrors? What action do you prioritize? What do you do with the rage? What constitutes self-care? If hedonism counts, when does it become self-abuse? The questions aren’t answered conclusively, but they play out compellingly. And like every Sylvan Esso album, things orbit around a few perfectly-conceived songs. The lead track “Entertainment & Coca-Cola” is an amuse-bouche, its conflicted pledge-of-allegiance to pleasure winking perhaps at Jean-Luc Godard’s famous quote and the carbonated tropicália of Caetano Veloso’s “Alegria, Alegria.” Similarly, the single “Hot Slob” echoes the meta-pop of Sylvan Esso signature “Radio,” but with a different sound—au courant ’90s alt-rock redux with ’70s-glam guitar punctuation. Character-actor air-quotes frame the song’s self-destructive narrator, maybe the pop savant from “Radio” or another over-exposed striver struggling with mommy issues, trying to navigate life’s lures

cards.source_text: “I’ll Fly Away” may be one of the most-sung songs of the 20th century. Written by a gospel composer named Albert Edward Brumley nearly 100 years ago, it’s been performed by congregations of various denominations and recorded by artists working in nearly every genre imaginable. It was originally a hit with gospel groups, including the Selah Jubilee Singers in the 1940s and, much later, the Staple Singers, but it’s been popular with country singers (George Jones, Alan Jackson) and blues artists (Rev. Gary Davis, Mississippi John Hurt), too. It’s been recorded by Johnny Cash, Jars of Clay, and Springsteen, although arguably the most popular version was sung by Alison Krauss and Gillian Welch for the O Brother, Where Art Thou? soundtrack. As of this writing, the web site SecondHandSongs lists more than 400 covers. For a song about soaring away from your troubles, that history weighs heavily: How do you sing “I’ll Fly Away” without gesturing in some way to its legacy? How do you make the audience hear it with fresh ears? Valerie June doesn’t completely solve that riddle, but the version that kicks off her new covers EP, Brighter Blue, certainly sounds refreshed: fleet in its tone and tempo, yet still burdened with worry. It opens with a strutting rhythm, like a jump blues slowed way down or a second line funeral march sped way up. The music is earthy and grounded, but it’s still funky and nimble, especially on a woozy pedal steel solo from Dan Iead. Valerie June takes nothing for granted in the song, and she hits notes Brumley never considered, her voice like a bird landing on unpopulated branches. No score yet, be the first to add. Crucially, there’s a sense of mischief in her delivery, which means there’s also a sense of self-determination. “I’ll Fly Away,” along with so many other hymns, is essentially about freedom and salvation deferred: This world is cruel, but we suffer through knowing we’ll accept our true reward in heaven. Valerie June sings like she’s devising a plan to get her reward in this life. Her interpretation feels especially timely when a deluge of bad news, pointless indignities, and stupid name changes can feel overwhelming and unstoppable. From her mouth “I’ll Fly Away” is a challenge, a call to arms. That’s an awful lot for one song to hold, and it’s a lot for a three-song EP to hold. While “the sound of mortar and machine gun, the collision of flesh and metal” are integral to Faulks’s best known works, such as Birdsong, in his 17th novel the military presence is a peacekeeping one. It’s 1946 and infantry officer Philip Deval, who saw action in Normandy, is deployed to the Holy Land to take part in maintaining Britain’s mandate in Palestine. Initially Philip is second in command of a battalion overseeing febrile relationships between Jewish and Arab communities. Britain’s profound failures and manipulation in the region, and the imminence of its disastrous departure from the territory, come under scrutiny. While able to drum up motivation and cheer for the men in his battalions, privately Philip wrestles with inner melancholy. He is “shrouded” in a “loneliness … that insulates him from the world”. Experiences on the battlefield and other, slowly elucidated tragedies have led to his pessimistic bent. Much of what Philip observes in the Middle East, and his “foreboding” sense of its intractable problems, only confirms his despairing sense of human nature. It also underlines his ambivalence towards notions of divine benevolence. In Jerusalem, Philip and some of his men find themselves in a raucous bar. cards.source_text: In the beginning, Art of Noise were as much a provocation as a pop group. You could tell something was up just by looking at the list of personnel: a computer programmer, a composer and arranger, a recording engineer, a producer, and a journalist. The band—some of them, anyway—played instruments that looked like space-station command centers, collecting bits of audio from everyday life and arranging them into block-rocking beats, with fragmentary voices criss-crossing in digitally orchestrated counterpoint and car engines standing in for tambourines. The music was sly and funny in a postmodern way that had only recently been enabled by the emergence of digital sampling technology. It delighted in its own fakeness; drew melodies out of non-musical detritus and used traditional instruments as punchlines; approached recorded sound itself as both pigment and canvas. There was no singing, per se, unless it had been chopped up and rearranged at the command center. They hardly performed in public and wore eerie kabuki-like masks in photographs. Somehow, they had a Top 10 hit. Paul Morley’s role in this startling enterprise was primarily a conceptual one: lore-enforcement agent, to use a title some troupe of cheeky youngsters really should nick for themselves, bestowed on him in a 1985 ZigZag magazine profile of ZTT Records, the swashbuckling avant-pop label for which Art of Noise served for a time as a sort of faceless avatar and house band. According to one Art of Noise member, interviewed about In Visible Silence, their strange, brilliant, and oft-overlooked second album, Morley’s only concrete contributions to the earlier releases were the names of the songs. It was just a few months after the ZigZag piece, but a schism within Art of Noise had transpired, one that the British press covered with a fervor it generally reserved for bands with lead singers. The lore-enforcement types were on one side and the people who made the records were on the other. No score yet, be the first to add. Morley was a former NME scribbler whose high-flying prose and messianic certitude could make a manifesto of a grocery list, to say nothing of an album review. In addition to Art of Noise’s track titles, he was responsible for the decision to frame them as a pop act in the first place, and for creating the conditions for listeners and the media to accept them as such. cards.source_text: You might assume that being a bad bitch is a universal language: one that transcends time, space, and social media to gag listeners both near and far. But when it comes to making oneself known, a closet full of high fashion and a metric tonne of attitude has proven to only ever be part of the equation. As American “A-Pop” plays catch-up to its Asian counterparts with military-precise, skibidi-brained slaying, the blueprint for a new kind of global performer has emerged. This new diva crosses borders, genres, and languages while keeping her cool intact; a proven star on her own turf who is flexible enough to incorporate regional and diasporic sounds and sensibilities without breaking a sweat. Whether they want to own their lane or conquer the charts, international pop acts who aim to assert themselves increasingly depend on acts of translation: distilling deep roots and local swagger into something unique and accessible for the whole world to hear. Helena Gao draws attention to this act of interpretation more dramatically than most. The Danish Chinese musician isn’t simply a bad girl, she’s niú bī (牛逼) and that distinction is both subtle and important. A fixture in Copenhagen’s alternative scene, Gao has lately become one of its most fascinating pop crossovers. She struck it big last year with her Grammy-nominated production on Zara Larsson’s Midnight Sun, lending a mother-of-pearl shimmer to the Swedish diva’s Viking-apocalypse belting. But in Asia, she’s best known for “Lao Shi,” an effervescent piece of dance-pop that became a viral hit on Douyin (aka TikTok). Zipping between lovestruck English verses and an unmistakably sexy Mandarin chorus (which translates to “teacher, teach me how to love”), the song was received both warmly and with some bafflement. The lyrics may initially scan as relatively tame by the standards of global pop, but some Chinese-speaking fans were shocked to hear such a forward perspective expressed in Mandarin. On Gao Dan Dan, her latest EP, the singer doubles down on boldness, taking her multi-cultural cool and concentrating it into a collection of bilingual pop gems. No score yet, be the first to add. Gao’s output has steadily evolved from vocal-driven folk-pop to unapologetic club fare, with the electronic flourishes that once underlined her songwriting becoming her most striking musical signature. cards.source_text: Three hours of music about water is an audacious proposition. But not, perhaps, for Slovak label Mappa, which for the past decade has made a habit of asking listeners to slow down and pay attention, releasing records that move between field recording, electronics, and idiosyncratic folk. Synthetic Water Music might be Mappa’s most expansive undertaking yet. The second installment in the label’s Synthetic series, following a 2023 collection dedicated to birds, it brings together several dozen artists whose contributions founder Jakub Juhás has arranged in a multi-layered journey through liquid states, aquatic environments, and drifting visions. While Synthetic Bird Music focused on animals and their sounds, both real and imagined, its successor treats water more elusively. It might be recorded directly, imitated electronically, or merely suggested by a voice, drone, or reverb. Sometimes it can’t be heard at all. Across the compilation, water becomes both sonic material and a starting point for constructing imagined hydrospheres. The material is spread across two cassettes, and Juhás has given each side the name of a fictional aquatic world: Tlālōcān, Nephelora, Žaboglach, and R’lyeh. Two are drawn from mythology, R’lyeh from the cosmic horror of H.P. Lovecraft, and Žaboglach is the curator’s own invention. Each one emphasizes a slightly different soundscape: Tlālōcān is brighter and more electronic, while Žaboglach leans toward swampland, darkness, and mud, with field recordings, electronic synthesis, and melodic fragments constantly shifting. Together, the four sides trace a descent from the surface and the life it sustains into the depths of the unknown. No score yet, be the first to add. The compilation is most compelling when real sounds become building blocks for worlds that exist only in the imagination. Pauline Anna Strom’s “Emerald Pool,” from 1982’s groundbreaking Trans-Millenia Consort—one of a number of archival releases Juhás has tapped for the album, alongside new commissions—combines synthesizers with recordings of ordinary, everyday phenomena, transforming them into fantastical sonic environments. The result is a phantasmagorical world in which synthesized harp and artificial voice merge with delicate sounds of water, creating an idyllic landscape that draws us into the album’s aquatic narrative. items.title: End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor review – the fightback starts here
items.summary: A sharp analysis of the damage wrought by the reckless super-rich, and progressive toolkit for repairing it The more power the radical rightwing nationalists of our age accrue, the greater the risk that their destructive brand of politics becomes normalised. We should not, for instance, regard it as normal that the man in charge of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals casually promises “a whole civilisation will die tonight”. We should not accept that history’s first trillionaire is allowed to spread racist conspiracy theories to a hitherto unimaginable extent. We should be alarmed that, here in the UK, a party tipped to lead a potential future government is trying to cruise to power in the slipstream of this international movement. In fact, we shouldn’t just be alarmed by such developments: we should stop them and urgently repair the damage already done. But how? And what is the nature of that damage? This bold, clarifying intervention from Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor provides some of the answers. “End times fascism” is their term for a convergence of interests that can broadly be understood as a response to the climate crisis. Faced with a world coming under unprecedented strain from environmental shocks and an unequal, resource-hungry economic system, today’s reactionaries are effectively saying: bring it on. items.title: Farewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks review – conflict and compromise, from a veteran of the genre
items.summary: A returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world war Sebastian Faulks’s latest book focuses on the most irreconcilable geopolitical struggle of our age, the Israel-Palestine conflict. While “the sound of mortar and machine gun, the collision of flesh and metal” are integral to Faulks’s best known works, such as Birdsong, in his 17th novel the military presence is a peacekeeping one. It’s 1946 and infantry officer Philip Deval, who saw action in Normandy, is deployed to the Holy Land to take part in maintaining Britain’s mandate in Palestine. Initially Philip is second in command of a battalion overseeing febrile relationships between Jewish and Arab communities. Britain’s profound failures and manipulation in the region, and the imminence of its disastrous departure from the territory, come under scrutiny. While able to drum up motivation and cheer for the men in his battalions, privately Philip wrestles with inner melancholy. He is “shrouded” in a “loneliness … that insulates him from the world”. Experiences on the battlefield and other, slowly elucidated tragedies have led to his pessimistic bent. Much of what Philip observes in the Middle East, and his “foreboding” sense of its intractable problems, only confirms his despairing sense of human nature. It also underlines his ambivalence towards notions of divine benevolence. Continue reading...
